source: Peirce (c.1903) Lectures on Pragmatism, CP 5.189, as summarised in SEP Abduction: Peirce
finding: Peirce's abduction schema is three lines: a surprising fact C is seen; if A were true, C would be a matter of course; so there is reason to suspect A. It is a rule for proposing a hypothesis worth testing, not for accepting it.
numbers: Three-line schema. Peirce worked on abduction for over fifty years, so his writings are not one coherent view.
quote: The surprising fact, C, is observed. But if A were true, C would be a matter of course. Hence, there is reason to suspect that A is true.
limits: Secondhand via SEP, not the Peirce text. Peirce never uses the idea of a 'best' explanation; that is a later addition.
agent_relevance: S3 (generate) should output a hypothesis plus the claim 'if A, then C is unsurprising', and S4 must then test A. Abduction alone is never acceptance.

source: SEP Abduction: Peirce - three stages and Frankfurt's reading
finding: Peirce's cycle: abduction forms explanatory hypotheses, deduction draws testable consequences, induction scores the hypothesis by how many consequences hold. Peirce called abduction the only logical operation that introduces a new idea (CP 5.172). Frankfurt reads abduction as choosing hypotheses worth investigating (a filter), not inventing them.
numbers: Three operations in a fixed order.
limits: Reading of Peirce is contested; this SEP page gives no detail on instinct or economy of research.
agent_relevance: Matches our loop S3 generate, deduce predictions, S4 test. The filter reading supports a cheap 'worth testing' screen before an expensive test.

source: Hanson (1960) via SEP Scientific Discovery sec 6.1
finding: Hanson's retroductive schema: surprising phenomena p1, p2, p3 are met; they would not be surprising if a hypothesis of type H held; so there is good reason to elaborate a hypothesis of type H. The output is a TYPE of hypothesis worth pursuing, not one specific hypothesis. His Kepler-Mars reconstruction is regarded as historically inadequate (Lugg 1985).
numbers: Three-step schema. SEP separates selective abduction (choose among known hypotheses) from creative abduction (generate new ones).
limits: The schema is silent on how a hypothesis is first conceived, and explanatory power alone is too permissive since many hypotheses explain the same data (Harman 1965). Logical only in the broad sense of 'rational'.
agent_relevance: Generate at the level of hypothesis TYPE first (cheap), then specialise. Keep selective and creative abduction as separate operators with different budgets.

source: SEP Scientific Discovery sec 5 and 6.2: context distinction and discovery machines
finding: The old view (Popper, linked to Reichenbach) split conceiving an idea from testing it and said only testing is open to logic. The 'discovery machine' objection (Curd 1980) says no rule can output good hypotheses mechanically. BACON and KEKADA (Simon et al.) found regularities from data by heuristic search, e.g. Kepler's third law and the Krebs cycle.
numbers: No numbers. Gillies (1996) argues such programs cannot decide which data are relevant.
limits: SEP does not link BACON or KEKADA to the abductive schema directly.
agent_relevance: Supports our split: the model guesses (discovery needs no logic), code does the testing. The agent does not need a logic of generation, only a reliable test.

source: Douven, SEP Abduction: schemas ABD1, ABD2, ABD3 and the bad lot
finding: ABD1 (textbook): infer the truth of the candidate that best explains E. Problems: 'candidate' and 'best' are undefined, and a comparative premise yields an absolute conclusion. ABD2 (Musgrave, Lipton) adds that the best must be 'good enough'. ABD3 (Kuipers) concludes only that the best is closer to the truth than the rest. Van Fraassen's 'best of a bad lot' objection hits ABD1; ABD2 and ABD3 mostly avoid it.
numbers: Three schemas. Lipton (1993) also proposed adding the negation of all considered hypotheses as a catch-all, which the entry calls hardly informative.
limits: Descriptive; no empirical test of which schema works.
agent_relevance: Supports our 'good enough threshold, checked by code' idea. Never output a comparative winner as a confident answer; require an absolute test pass (G3, G6).

source: Douven, SEP Abduction: Bayes versus IBE, van Fraassen, Lipton's compromise
finding: Van Fraassen: a more informative theory cannot be more probable, and probabilistic abduction either equals Bayes' rule or is Dutch-bookable. Replies: Maher and Skyrms (losses in one respect offset by gains in another); Douven 1999 (coherence belongs to packages of epistemic and decision rules). Lipton: Bayesians should be explanationists, using virtues to set priors and likelihoods. Heuristic view (Okasha, McGrew, Lipton, Dellsen): explanatory power guides priors when one would otherwise guess. Psillos: abduction picks hypotheses to test, Bayes then tests them.
numbers: No numbers. Entry cites Douven & Schupbach 2015 (updates influenced by explanation, deviating from Bayes) and Douven 2016b (people weighting explanation more were more accurate under a standard scoring rule).
limits: Entry reports Douven's simulations only qualitatively. 'Neighbour problem': a Bayesian can already set priors for any reason, so Lipton's advice has little bite.
agent_relevance: Gives virtues a role as cheap priors over candidates, with the real update done by tests. Fits G5 if virtues are computed by code, not judged by the model.

source: Douven, SEP Abduction: explanatory virtues and psychology
finding: Common virtues: simplicity, generality, coherence with accepted theory (Thagard 1978, McMullin 1996). Giere says they lack content; SEP says formal work on simplicity (Forster & Sober 1994) and coherence (Bovens & Hartmann 2003) makes that hard to hold. Schupbach & Sprenger (2011) define explanatory power probabilistically. Lombrozo (2007): people overrate simple explanations. Koslowski et al. (2008): background coherence matters.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Formal measures are contested (Dellsen & Trpin 2025 footnote cites Lange 2022 arguing no general measure exists).
agent_relevance: Virtues code can compute: parsimony (count of assumptions), scope (observations covered), fit (held-out likelihood). Unification cannot be computed; do not ask the model to judge it.

source: Lombrozo (2007) Simplicity and probability in causal explanation, Cognitive Psychology 55, Experiment 1
finding: With no base rates given, 96% of participants chose the one-cause explanation of two symptoms over two-cause alternatives, and 92% chose the more probable disease when base rates were given. Simplicity decides when probability is silent.
numbers: N=48 undergraduates. Simplicity condition 96% chose one-cause (binomial p<.01 vs chance). Probability condition 92% chose the more probable disease. Of the 96%, justifications: 17% simplicity, 39% sufficiency, 39% probability.
limits: Alien-disease vignettes; people may infer equal base rates, which is why Exp 2 supplied them. One elite university.
agent_relevance: A model, like a person, will likely lean to the simpler story when no numbers are given. Supply counts so the choice rests on data, not on that default.

source: Lombrozo (2007) Experiment 2: simplicity versus probability
finding: With base rates, people traded simplicity against probability but kept a bias toward the simple explanation. Logistic fit: slope 0.795 (SE .217, not different from the ideal 1), constant -1.306 (SE .248, p<.01). So probability was not underweighted; the bias sits in the PRIOR, estimated at 79% for the simpler explanation.
numbers: N=144. 71% chose the simpler explanation overall; base-rate condition mattered, chi2(7)=25, p<.01. Even when the two-cause explanation was 10 times more likely, over a third chose the simple one. Justifications: 51% probability, 15% simplicity, 13% sufficiency. 69% passed a math check.
limits: Non-probabilistic accounts (Thagard; Read and Marcus-Newhall) predict always-simple; data refute that. The prior reading is one of two fits.
agent_relevance: Simplicity acts like a prior (about 4 to 1 odds for the simple story), not a deciding rule. Encode a virtue as a prior in code and let evidence override it.

source: Lombrozo (2007) Experiment 3: consequences of committing to the simple explanation
finding: Replication of Exp 2 as a computer task with 75 aliens. Simple choice 63% overall; at a 1:10 ratio (simple 10 times less likely) 41% still chose it. Slope 0.62 (SE .157), constant -0.77 (SE .24); implied prior 68% (CI 57 to 78%). People who committed to the simple story overestimated how common its single cause was: 19% vs 8% at 1:2 (p<.05) and 29% vs 10% at 1:10 (suggestive).
numbers: Matched Exp 2 at 15:1 (96 vs 94%), 1:2 (56 vs 67%), 1:10 (41 vs 39%); differed at 9:10. Less simplicity bias than Exp 2 on one comparison: 59 vs 89%, chi2(1)=4.6, p<.05.
limits: Frequency estimates are noisy with unequal variance (t df 14.6). The prior estimate dropped from 79% to 68% across versions.
agent_relevance: Committing to an explanation distorts later estimates. Matches G1 and G2: do not let the model re-estimate from its own chosen story; recompute from raw counts.

source: Lombrozo (2007) Experiment 4: ambiguity and the use of simplicity
finding: The simplicity preference shrinks when probability information is unambiguous. When the complex story was stated as joint probability, only 17% chose the simple one; when stated as simply likely, 46%; versus 61% at the matching ratio in Exp 2.
numbers: N=48. Joint-probability condition 17% vs 61% in Exp 2 (chi2(1)=8.85, p<.01). Likely condition 46% vs 17% joint (chi2(1)=4.75, p<.05); vs Exp 2 61% not different (p>.2). 75% passed the math check.
limits: Small N per cell. Between-experiment comparisons use different participants.
agent_relevance: Make evidence unambiguous (explicit counts, joint probabilities) before asking for a choice; simplicity bias shows mainly when evidence is vague.

source: Lombrozo (2016) Explanatory preferences shape learning and inference, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 20(10)
finding: Review of experiments on simplicity and breadth. Choices depend on both simplicity and probability when probability is uncertain; children aged 4 to 6 mirror adults. Adults showed no simplicity preference in a child-friendly task with transparent numbers, so simplicity informs inference only when reliable probability guides are absent. Best measure of simplicity is the fewest unexplained causes (root simplicity), not the raw number of causes.
numbers: A majority chose the complex explanation only when it was 10-fold more likely. Root simplicity beat node simplicity in experiments cited as [16] in the review. Narrower latent scope (fewer unverified predictions) was preferred, replicated with children.
limits: Review, secondhand numbers, no sample sizes. Causal-learning work on a preference for few strong causes has conflicting results (the review's [30]).
agent_relevance: For code-computed parsimony, count unexplained assumptions (roots), not steps. This is a concrete checkable definition. Also penalise unverified predictions (latent scope).

source: Lombrozo (2016) TICS: explaining changes learning and inference
finding: Prompting people to explain pushes them toward simple and broad hypotheses. Five-year-olds prompted to explain more often chose the common-cause hypothesis than those prompted to report; 4-year-olds were at chance in both groups. Adults prompted to explain more often discovered a subtle rule covering all eight study items than description, think-aloud or free-study controls. Explaining can also hinder learning when a partial rule is adopted.
numbers: Category task, three experiments: a '75% rule' covers 75% of exemplars, the '100% rule' covers all. Explainers were significantly more likely than every control group to find the 100% rule.
limits: Effects may be reduced in older children who explain spontaneously. No sample sizes in the review.
agent_relevance: Asking a model to explain may push it toward its first simple pattern. Use explanation to find a pattern, then test it against all items before trusting it (G3).

source: Douven & Schupbach (2015) Probabilistic alternatives to Bayesianism: the case of explanationism, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: In a two-urn study (reanalysed from Schupbach 2011), credences were predicted better by objective probabilities plus people's own explanatory judgments than by objective probabilities alone. People are not strict Bayesians; explanatory goodness shifts credence, even beyond calculated measures of explanatory power.
numbers: N=26, 10 draws without replacement from one of two 40-ball urns (A: 30 black, 10 white; B: 15 black, 25 white). Model with explanatory judgments MOAB: R2=0.90 vs 0.83 for Bayes-only MO; AIC gap over 120; chi2(2)=124.87, p<0.0001. Best calculated measure (Good, rescaled alpha=2): AIC -446.83, R2 0.86; coefficients O .40, A .24, B -.13.
limits: Small N. Regression is descriptive: it shows deviation from Bayes, not that deviation is more accurate. The article leaves the bonus size unspecified and gives no accuracy comparison.
agent_relevance: Explanation-based credence shifts are human behaviour, not proof of truth-tracking. Do not copy them into the agent unless a held-out test shows gain (G7).

source: Pettigrew (2021) On the pragmatic and epistemic virtues of IBE, Synthese: the EXPL rule
finding: Douven's EXPL rule: posterior is prior times likelihood plus a fixed bonus c split equally among the best explanations of the TOTAL evidence, then normalised. With c=0 it is exactly Bayes. In a 3-ball urn with equal priors and one violet draw, Bayes gives H1 2/3 while EXPL gives (2+6c)/(3+6c).
numbers: Worked example: 2/3 for Bayes versus (2+6c)/(3+6c) > 2/3 for c>0.
limits: Secondhand from a critic who defends Bayes. EXPL acts on total evidence, which separates it from conditionalisation.
agent_relevance: EXPL is a concrete code-computable bonus for the best-fitting candidate and is cheap to implement. Whether it helps is the next line.

source: Pettigrew (2021) on Douven's urn simulations: speed versus expected accuracy
finding: Convergence sim: 10-ball urn, hypotheses H0 to H10, uniform prior, 500 draws per sequence, 1000 sequences per hypothesis; EXPL reached credence above 0.9 in the truth sooner than Bayes for every hypothesis. Accuracy sim (Douven 2021): 1000 draws, 1000 sequences, Brier score at 100, 250, 500, 750, 1000 draws; EXPL more often more accurate at every checkpoint, especially for extreme hypotheses. Pettigrew: EXPL wins most runs by small margins, Bayes wins the rest by large margins, so Bayes has higher EXPECTED accuracy.
numbers: Threshold 0.9. A deliberately dumb rule that waits 10 draws then jumps to the matching hypothesis scores equal or better on the speed metric.
limits: Win-rate and expected score give opposite verdicts. Pettigrew argues the games are rigged because nobody acts at exactly 0.9.
agent_relevance: Choose the comparison metric before comparing selectors. Report both win-rate and expected score; use expected correct answers per token as arbiter (G7).

source: Douven & Wenmackers (2017) IBE versus Bayes' rule in a social setting (BJPS), as reported by Pettigrew 2021
finding: Agents update on world evidence, then average with peers within a bounded-confidence interval delta (Hegselmann-Krause model). Authors report EXPL beats Bayes on most hypotheses. Pettigrew's critique: the Bayes arm used averaging, the wrong tool there; geometric pooling (Baccelli & Stewart) reproduces the Bayes result without extracting the evidence.
numbers: c and delta each varied 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1; Brier score. Some EXPL setting with some delta beats Bayes with any delta on most hypotheses.
limits: Original paper not opened; a talk abstract claims IBE beats Bayes on every criterion. The comparison is contested as unfair to Bayes.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that an explanation bonus helps when agents share beliefs. Relevant to G4/G9: pooling other samples is not independent evidence.

source: Trpin & Pellert (2019) IBE in uncertain evidential situations (BJPS): IBE** versus Jeffrey conditionalization
finding: With uncertain evidence (coin outcomes seen at confidence 0.6 to 0.9), the IBE-style agent assigned high probability to the true coin far more often than the Jeffrey agent, but was also more often confident in a false hypothesis. Jeffrey's Brier score worsened over rounds (0.77 to 1.06) while IBE**'s improved (0.35 to 0.02).
numbers: 55,000 simulations: 1000 per coin, 11 coins, 5 lighting levels, up to 1500 updates. IBE** Pr(true)>0.95 or 0.99 in about half the runs (49% to 52%) vs 11% to 16% for JC (table columns garbled in extraction). Confident in a false hypothesis: IBE** 30% and 22% vs JC 24% and 17%. Brier by round: IBE** 0.35, 0.12, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02; JC 0.77, 0.86, 0.97, 1.03, 1.06.
limits: Coin toy world with a fixed, correct hypothesis set. IBE** is bolder: more confident in truth AND in falsehood. Not about generating hypotheses.
agent_relevance: An explanation-bonus selector gains speed at the cost of more confident errors. Use only where a code check can catch the confident-wrong cases.

source: Dellsen & Trpin (2025) Testing Abductions From Uncertain Evidence (Philosophical Quarterly)
finding: Compares Basic IBE (use all evidence), Filtered IBE (use only evidence above a certainty threshold) and Evidentially Robust IBE (infer only what follows from every best explanation across plausible readings of the evidence, often a hedged disjunction). No rule wins everywhere. Robust IBE wins when evidence is uncertain, the hypothesis space is large (7 or 11 coins) and errors cost more than correct answers pay. Basic and Filtered win when the task is simple, evidence is clean or a bold guess is cheap.
numbers: 5,460 simulation settings, 1,000 rounds each. Tosses 10, 25, 50, 100; hypotheses 3, 7, 11; thresholds 0.5 to 0.9; reward and penalty combos from 0, 1, 2, 10. A true claim earns k/m (share of false hypotheses ruled out); a false claim costs p. Low-risk easy task (100 tosses, 3 hypotheses, reward 10, penalty 0) favours bold rules; high-risk hard task (10 tosses, 11 hypotheses, reward 0, penalty 10) favours Robust IBE.
limits: Assumes a fixed correct hypothesis list and picks the best explanation by maximum likelihood, so it says nothing about the bad-lot problem. Coin world only.
agent_relevance: Design rule for S7: when evidence is noisy and wrong answers are costly, answer with what all top candidates agree on, not the single top pick; when tests are clean and cheap, commit to the top pick. G6 still applies: hedge, do not submit nothing.

source: Dellsen (2020) Explanatory Consolidation: From 'Best' to 'Good Enough' (PPR)
finding: Standard IBE (Lipton 2004) is two stages: generate hypotheses, infer the best (greatest balance of virtues). 'Good enough' read as a loveliness threshold has three problems, the first being that absolute virtue levels cannot be measured or accessed during reasoning. Dellsen proposes a third stage: the best becomes a working hypothesis and turns 'good enough' only through explanatory consolidation, as evidence accumulates and attempts to find a better rival fail (Fresnel's wave theory is the example).
numbers: Three-stage model: (i) generate, (ii) adopt the loveliest as working hypothesis, (iii) consolidate over time. No empirical numbers.
quote: more a slogan than an articulated philosophical theory
limits: Philosophical argument; consolidation is a process with no sharp cut-off.
agent_relevance: A template for our loop: S3/S7 pick a working hypothesis; S4/S8 consolidate by surviving distinct tests plus a bounded search for rivals that finds none. Define 'good enough' as that, checked by code.

source: Dellsen (2020) on Lipton's loveliness versus likeliness
finding: Following Lipton (2004), 'loveliness' is the balance of explanatory virtues (simplicity or parsimony, scope, unification, fit with background data); 'better' means lovelier. 'Likeliness' is probability of truth. Lipton's IBE says loveliness guides likeliness. Dellsen notes Lipton hinted goodness may be comparative, not absolute, but left it undeveloped.
numbers: Virtues named: simplicity, explanatory scope, unificatory power, fit with background data.
limits: Secondhand account of Lipton, not Lipton's book. Whether loveliness tracks likeliness is the open empirical question; the Angle B/C files of this subfield cover it.
agent_relevance: Keep two numbers per candidate: loveliness (code-computed virtue score) and likeliness (test pass rate on held-out data). Never let the first replace the second (G3, G8).

source: Sun & Saparov (2025) Do Language Models Follow Occam's Razor? (InAbHyD), arXiv 2509.03345
finding: Synthetic benchmark: the model gets an incomplete ontology plus observations and must propose hypotheses that explain them. LLMs do well on shallow trees with one hypothesis, fall sharply with several, and a persistent gap remains between valid hypotheses (explain everything) and simplest-correct hypotheses (match ground truth).
numbers: Over 2K questions, tree height 1 to 4, 500 per height, 3.0 to 6.6 ground-truth hypotheses. Height 1: all models above 80% weak and strong accuracy. Height 1 to 2: above 80% to below 50% for all models except GPT-4o. Height 4: at least 20% weak accuracy, very low strong accuracy and quality. Parsimony metric agreed with annotators 79% (random 33.3%, length heuristic 51%, Fleiss kappa 0.75).
quote: LLMs can perform inductive and abductive reasoning at high accuracy for shallow ontology trees with a single hypothesis.
limits: Model names as printed in the page (GPT-5.4, o3, Llama3-70B, Gemma3-27B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, R1-Distill-Llama-70B). Per-model values are in figures I could not read. Fictional clean worlds.
agent_relevance: Models produce explanations that fit but are not minimal, the bad-lot and parsimony problem in a model. A code-side parsimony measure (reuse of hypotheses across proofs) can pick among valid candidates.

source: Sun & Saparov (2025) InAbHyD: error types, prompting, in-context learning
finding: Four common errors: wrong direction of a relation, unnecessary hypotheses that ignore the ontology, trivial hypotheses that restate the observations, and hallucinated entities (often copied from demonstrations). 8-shot in-distribution demonstrations helped slightly at heights 3 and 4; out-of-distribution ones gave no significant gain. Buffer-of-thought generally beat chain-of-thought, especially on weak accuracy. Reasoning models beat Llama3-70B.
numbers: Gemma3-27B at height 4: near 50% weak accuracy on membership tasks but about 10% on subtype tasks.
limits: The abstract mentions RLVR but the text read reports no separate RLVR run.
agent_relevance: Trivial-restatement and unneeded-hypothesis errors are cheap to detect in code (does a hypothesis only repeat the data; is each part used in some proof). Add them as S4 filters.

source: He et al. (2025) GEAR: A General Evaluation Framework for Abductive Reasoning, arXiv 2509.24096
finding: Scores hypothesis SETS without gold answers, by consistency (explains the observations), generalizability (determinate predictions on unseen inputs) and diversity (distinct predictions across the set). Draws on Peirce's generation view, Popper (riskier claims) and Chamberlin's multiple working hypotheses. Nine LLMs, four benchmarks: 50,340 hypotheses, 17,835 consistent; of the 32,505 rest, 4,346 had format failures and 28,159 contradicted an observation.
numbers: Nine LLMs, four benchmarks (MINI-ARC, ACRE, LIST FUNCTIONS, ARC-2025), 1,500 problems. 70B-class models gave only about 20% consistent hypotheses; consistency did not correlate with number of observations; model size weakly related to diversity; about 80% of equally plausible hypotheses are marked wrong by gold-answer scoring. Consistent hypotheses reach about 95% coverage.
limits: Programmable domains only; natural-language settings need a semantic equivalence step.
agent_relevance: This is generate-then-test as an evaluation: run each hypothesis on the observations (consistency), then on unseen inputs (generalisation). Use the same three code-computed scores in S4/S7 and keep a diverse set rather than one gold answer.

source: He et al. (2025) GEAR: label-free training and momentum curriculum
finding: Turning GEAR scores into 839,522 preference pairs and training with DPO (LoRA rank 128) raised diversity and top-k accuracy on held-out problems; a momentum curriculum beat a fixed-ratio mix. Llama-3.1-8b top-1 0.000 to 0.028 and top-3 0.004 to 0.049 with the curriculum; instruction following 0.149 to about 0.97.
numbers: 839,522 preference pairs. Absolute top-k gains are small on the 8B model. A paper simulation says more diverse hypothesis sets are more likely to predict hidden observations.
limits: Training, not a scaffold; our agent cannot train. Qwen-2.5-7b consistency was already 0.987 before training.
agent_relevance: Evidence for keeping hypothesis sets diverse: diverse sets predict hidden observations better. Supports several distinct hypotheses at S3, scored by tests, rather than near-duplicate best-of-N (G4).

source: Bhagavatula et al. (2019) Abductive Commonsense Reasoning (ART, alphaNLI), arXiv 1908.05739
finding: First large benchmark of abduction in narrative text: choose or write the most plausible explanation linking two observations. Models lagged humans widely.
numbers: ART: over 20k contexts and 200k explanations. Abductive NLI: human 91.4%, best model 68.9%, gap 22.5 points.
limits: Abstract page only; 2019 models. The gold answer is one annotator-preferred hypothesis, which GEAR says hides underdetermination.
agent_relevance: Historical baseline. Newer LLMs likely close much of this gap; do not rely on this number for current models.

source: Del & Fishel (2023) True Detective: a deep abductive reasoning benchmark, arXiv 2212.10114
finding: 191 long detective mysteries (about 1,200 words each, mostly four options). Plain prompting is near chance; chain-of-thought helps GPT-4 only; giving the author's reasoning chain lifts GPT-4 to near the best humans, so the weak step is producing the reasoning, not the final choice.
numbers: Vanilla: GPT-3.5 FeedME 0.28, PPO 0.26, GPT-4 0.27. CoT: 0.26, 0.29, 0.38. Golden CoT: 0.46, 0.63, 0.83. Random 0.24; average human 0.47; top humans 0.8 to 0.9.
limits: Zero-shot, 2022 to 2023 models. Human average 47% may reflect ill-posed mysteries. Mystery length did not predict GPT-4 success.
agent_relevance: With a correct reasoning chain the model chooses well; the bottleneck is producing and ranking explanations. Supports generate-many then test over one long chain.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models, arXiv 2309.05660
finding: Generate-then-test: the model proposes several natural-language hypotheses, implements each as a Python program, runs them on observed examples, then applies survivors to new inputs. Hypotheses are filtered by LLM summary or human pick.
numbers: Random 100-problem ARC subset: direct prompting 17%; automated pipeline with LLM summaries 30%; with human selection of candidates 33%. Also tested on 1D-ARC, SyGuS, List Functions.
limits: Abstract page only. Small subset; human selection is not available to our agent. Ablations say both abstract hypotheses and program form help.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our S3/S4: nearly doubling accuracy (17% to 30%) by hypothesis generation, execution on examples and filtering. Fits G3 if a held-out example is also checked.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: iterative hypothesis refinement, arXiv 2310.08559
finding: Propose a rule, test it on examples, refine from failures. It helps on some tasks, not all. The model is a good rule proposer but a poor rule applier when it must run the rule itself: with a symbolic interpreter MiniSCAN task accuracy is 85.0, with the LM as interpreter 0.0.
numbers: GPT-4 MiniARC raw/task: IO 33.1/13.8; self-consistency N=5 31.3/13.1; self-refine 15.1/9.2; hypothesis refinement T=3,N=5 18.7/14.6; T=1,N=1 5.9/3.8. Best refinement: ACRE 82.5/59.0; MiniSCAN 93.3/85.0; List Functions 71.2/61.2. MiniSCAN task, symbolic vs LM interpreter: GPT-3.5 8.0 to 0.0; Claude-2 13.0 to 0.0. List Functions noise (T=1,N=1): 42.4 at 0% noise, 38.8 at 12.5%, 23.6 at 25%, 12.4 at 50%.
limits: Older models. Refinement tends to add exceptions to a wrong rule and fails when the first hypothesis is entirely off. Text read to 100k of 125k characters.
agent_relevance: Run the hypothesis in code; never ask the model to apply its own rule (G2, G5). A wrong first hypothesis needs a fresh restart, not patching: matches our S6 impasse and reframe.

source: Floridi, Morley, Novelli & Watson (2025) What kind of reasoning (if any) is an LLM actually doing? arXiv 2512.10080
finding: Conceptual argument that token-completion LLMs do not perform abduction; output looks abductive because training text encodes human reasoning. LLMs produce plausible hypotheses but cannot discern truth or verify explanations, so outputs must be examined.
numbers: No measured results; examples only.
limits: Philosophical position paper, not an experiment. Treat as a view, not data.
agent_relevance: Agrees with our split: the model supplies candidate explanations; verification is external (G10).
